water-wastewater-technology.figs_h2: Water and wastewater: the figures behind demand
water-wastewater-technology.figs_intro: Demand for water technology is driven by regulation and by the condition of rivers, plants and pipes. The figures below come from China’s national statistics, Chinese city bulletins and the European Commission.
facts: Of 3,641 national surface-water monitoring sections in China, 91.4% were rated good (Classes I–III) in 2025; 0.6% were rated worse than Class V.
The EU counts 30,354 urban wastewater treatment plants in operation, and says 10 million Europeans still lack access to basic sanitation services.

The revised EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive entered into force on 1 January 2025. It requires collection and treatment in all urban areas of more than 1,000 inhabitants and stricter treatment, including for new pollutants.
The recast EU Drinking Water Directive (EU) 2020/2184 introduces a risk-based monitoring model aimed at emerging pollutants such as PFAS and microplastics.
Taizhou in Zhejiang made 64.0521 million pumps in 2025 (−2.0%) and 232,000 tonnes of valves (−3.2%).
water-wastewater-technology.figs_after: Stricter rules abroad translate into more detailed questions for suppliers: what a membrane removes, what a pump’s wetted materials are, whether components are approved for drinking water. Suppliers who publish those answers save buyers a round of emails, and get shortlisted earlier.

water-wastewater-technology.std_intro: Which approvals apply depends on the product and the country. These are the references overseas water buyers most often bring up.
standards: NSF/ANSI 61 sets minimum health-effects requirements for contaminants that products and materials can impart to drinking water. Its scope covers mechanical devices such as water meters, valves and filters, pipes and fittings, and process media such as filter media and ion-exchange resins. It does not set performance requirements.

The recast EU Drinking Water Directive applies to water for domestic purposes and food production, from tap, tanker or bottle, and sets thresholds that the Commission says are often stricter than WHO guidelines.
The revised EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive pushes for more nutrient removal, water reuse and resource recovery, and lower greenhouse-gas emissions from plants.
Pumps, blowers and other machinery sold in the EU fall under the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC; the new Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027.

textiles-technical-fabrics.std_intro: Textile compliance is product- and market-specific. These are the references that come up most often with buyers in Europe and North America.
standards: OEKO-TEX® STANDARD 100 certifies textiles tested for harmful substances; every thread, button and accessory is tested against a list of over 1,000 substances, with four product classes from baby articles to decoration materials.
OEKO-TEX says its certification covers requirements including Annexes XVII and XIV of REACH, CPSIA and the ECHA candidate list of substances of very high concern.

The EU’s Textile Labelling Regulation (EU) 1007/2011 requires textile products to be labelled or marked with their fibre composition whenever they are made available on the market; it does not cover size, origin or care labelling.
REACH (EC 1907/2006) is the main EU law on chemical risks; it places responsibility on industry to manage the risks of the substances it uses.
The EU’s Digital Product Passport will be introduced product group by product group; the Commission’s timeline lists textiles for an ecodesign delegated act in 2027.

Which tests has this fabric passed?

What is your MOQ and how fast can you sample?

Can you prove recycled or organic content?

Can you develop a custom fabric?
Explain your development process, lab capability and how long a new article typically takes.
How do you ship and to where?

Under SOLAS, port State control lets governments inspect foreign ships if there are clear grounds to believe the ship or its equipment does not comply.

Equipment carried on EU-flagged ships must comply with the Marine Equipment Directive 2014/90/EU. EMSA’s MED Portal lists more than 200,000 approved marine equipment items, and its MED e-tag lets manufacturers link certified products to the portal with a Data Matrix code.

automotive-mobility-components.std_intro: These references come up most with OEM, Tier 1 and European aftermarket buyers:
standards: ISO/TS 16949 was created in 1999 by the International Automotive Task Force to harmonise assessment and certification systems across the automotive supply chain; IATF 16949:2016 replaced it and stays aligned with ISO 9001.
Regulation (EU) 2018/858 governs the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles and of systems, components and separate technical units intended for them.

The EU End-of-Life Vehicles Regulation, which the Commission announced on 12 August 2026 was entering into force, sets recycled-plastic targets for new vehicles of 15% from 2032 and 25% from 2036, with targets for steel and aluminium to follow from 2033.

The EU Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 covers electric-vehicle and other batteries, including those built into vehicles, with rules on safety, labelling, supply-chain due diligence and end of life.
From 18 February 2027 a digital product passport becomes mandatory for certain batteries, including electric-vehicle batteries.

buyer_q: Are you IATF 16949 certified?
Show the certificate, the site it covers, the scope and the certification body.
Which OEM or Tier 1 programmes do you supply?
Name them only with permission; otherwise describe the vehicle segment and component.
Can you meet PPAP and APQP requirements?
Explain your launch process, documentation and sample submission levels.
Which parts carry E-mark or other approvals?
List approvals per part number, never as a blanket claim.
What is your capacity and tooling lead time?
Annual capacity per process, tooling ownership and typical lead times.
Can you cross-reference OE numbers?
For aftermarket parts, a searchable OE and fitment table saves buyers days.
automotive-mobility-components.play_intro: Engineering, quality and purchasing each look for different proof. Our usual order:

Give each part family a page with drawings or specification tables, materials, tolerances, test standards and part numbers in HTML, not only in PDFs.
Publish a quality page: IATF 16949 and ISO certificates, PPAP levels, measurement and test equipment, and traceability.
For EV parts, add pages that explain battery-regulation and passport questions factually, with links to the official sources.
For aftermarket ranges, build OE cross-reference and fitment pages that search engines can read.
Use an RFQ form that asks for drawing or OE number, annual volume, material, target market and start of production.
Measure which systems and markets bring qualified RFQs in Search Console and analytics, and deepen those pages first.

faq: Do overseas automotive buyers really source online?
Yes. Engineers search by part, material, process and approval, and check your website before an audit.
Should we publish part numbers and drawings?
Publish part numbers and drawings you own. Keep customer drawings and confidential programmes off the site.
Can we say we supply a well-known car brand?
Only with written permission. Otherwise describe the vehicle segment, the component and the volume.
Do we need IATF 16949 before we market abroad?
OEM and Tier 1 programmes usually ask for it; many aftermarket buyers accept ISO 9001 with strong test data. Say exactly what you hold.
How should aftermarket suppliers handle OE numbers?
Use OE numbers as cross-references, state that parts are replacements, and keep fitment data accurate and up to date.
Will you guarantee rankings or orders?
No. We improve how buyers find and evaluate you, and we report real search and enquiry data.
